items.prompt: A radio report says the world economies have grown closer through trade, travel and technology. Define globalisation.
items.canonical_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of the economies of the world: trade in goods and services across borders widens, companies spread their production and sales across several countries, and information, finance and people move between countries more freely. It names a process, not a single event.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state the growing integration of the world economies and name what moves between countries - goods and services, companies operating across borders, information, finance and people.
A definition that names a single cause, such as technology alone, is partial credit at most: the term covers trade, companies and the movement of people and information together.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: At a supermarket in Oshakati a learner finds rice from Vietnam, a phone designed in Japan, and a banking app that moves money to a cousin studying in Portugal. Identify two features of globalisation these examples show.
items.canonical_answer: Feature one: goods produced in one country and sold in others - the rice from Vietnam and the phone designed in Japan crossed borders to reach the shelf. Feature two: information and finance moving worldwide - the banking app sends money between Namibia and Portugal in seconds. Both are features of globalisation: cross-border ties in goods, in companies and in the movement of people and their money.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark per feature of globalisation identified from the scenario, tied to the example that shows it.

What it includes: the features the examples can support are trade across borders, companies producing in several countries, and information and finance moving worldwide - a feature named without its example earns partial credit at most.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Haneda Electronics keeps its head office in Japan and runs assembly plants in Oshakati and in Brazil. Define a multinational company.
items.canonical_answer: A multinational company is a firm that produces goods or sells them in more than one country. The country of its head office is its home country, and each country where it produces or sells is a host country - here Japan is home, and Namibia and Brazil are hosts. What makes the firm multinational is where it operates, not who owns it or how large it is.
marking_guidance: Definition: the precise meaning required is producing or selling in more than one country, with the home country named as the head office country and the others as host countries.

The boundary to insist on: a multinational company is defined by where it operates, not by ownership - a public limited company sells shares on a stock exchange, a state-owned company belongs to a government, and the same firm may be multinational and either of these. The test is which question the sentence answers: ownership traded, who owns it, or where it operates.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Marula Foods of Windhoek is considering opening a jam factory near Lisbon in Portugal. Explain why producing in another country may suit the firm.
items.canonical_answer: Producing in Portugal may suit Marula Foods for several linked reasons. Costs: wages and fruit near Lisbon may be lower than in Namibia, so producing there may cost less per jar. Distance: a factory in Portugal sits close to European buyers, so transport costs and delivery times fall, and a European buyer may prefer a supplier whose goods cross no ocean. Markets: selling is easier from within a region, because the firm serves customers directly and may answer their tastes faster. Each reason is a purpose of the move: lower costs, closer customers, and a wider market reached more easily.
marking_guidance: Reasons: award one mark per reason and one for its development with a because link - lower costs, closer customers, transport savings, or wider markets.
Why: the reason must be the firm purpose, not a fact about Portugal - a developed reason states what the location does for the firm.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Haneda Electronics, with its head office in Japan, employs 300 workers at its new Oshakati plant at an average N$6 500 a month and has trained 60 technicians whose skills are now used by other firms in the town. Its profits, about N$12 million a year, are paid to the head office. Explain what the figures suggest about the effects of this multinational company on its host country.
items.canonical_answer: The figures suggest the host country gains and pays in the same breath. The plant pays 300 workers an average N$6 500 a month, which means that wages worth about N$2 million a month reach Oshakati households. The 60 trained technicians are a gain that spreads: because their skills are used by other firms in the town, the training raises local know-how beyond the plant itself. The cost the figures also show: about N$12 million of profit is paid to the head office each year, which means that part of the value created in Namibia leaves the host economy as it is remitted home.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must work from the figures - the 300 jobs at N$6 500, the 60 technicians, and the N$12 million profit - rather than from general knowledge of multinational companies.
Reasoning: each effect needs its because link - jobs and wages because the plant employs locally, skills because training spreads to other firms, outflow because profit is paid to the head office.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean that for the host country: gains in jobs, wages and skills, alongside profit leaving for the home country.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: After Namibia ended its border taxes on imported shoes, a learner says the shoes are now free goods. Define free trade.
items.canonical_answer: Free trade is international trade without government barriers: no tariffs on imports, no import quotas, no embargoes. The word free refers to the absence of barriers, not to the goods being free of charge - the imported shoes still carry a price and their buyers still pay it, so they are not free goods, which are goods so abundant that taking them costs nothing.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state international trade without barriers - tariffs, import quotas and embargoes - and may add that free refers to the barriers rather than to price.

The confusion to correct: free trade is a border policy while a free good is a good with no opportunity cost; the test is whether the sentence is about what happens at the border or about what the good costs. The learner in the prompt has run the two together.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why consumers in Namibia tend to gain when the country trades freely.
items.canonical_answer: Consumers tend to gain in two ways. Prices: with imports entering without tariffs or quotas, home sellers face competitors whose goods cost the border price, and competition tends to pull prices down - a consumer buying a blanket pays less because a cheaper import sits on the next shelf. Choice: free trade brings goods the home country does not make, or makes in fewer varieties, so a consumer chooses from a wider range. Both are benefits to individuals as consumers; the country as a whole gains separately, as resources shift towards what Namibia produces best.
marking_guidance: Reasons: award one mark per reason - lower prices through import competition, wider choice - and one for its development with a because link.

The level to keep: these are benefits to individuals as consumers, which differ from benefits to the country as a whole - the answer should name who gains, and a response about the whole economy answers a different question.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Before Namibia removed a tariff, imported blankets cost N$250 each and home blankets N$240. After the removal, imported blankets cost N$200 and home blankets N$210, and the number of blanket brands in the shops rose from 6 to 14. Explain how consumers in this economy gain from the removal, using the figures.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show the gains landing on consumers directly. Prices: the imported blanket falls from N$250 to N$200, and the home blanket falls from N$240 to N$210, because home makers can no longer price under the tariff-sheltered import - the consumer saves N$40 on a home blanket and N$50 on an imported one. Choice: brands rise from 6 to 14, which means that varieties the tariff kept out now reach the shops. Together the figures mean that freer trade gives consumers lower prices and a wider choice, as import competition reaches the shelf.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - N$250 to N$200, N$240 to N$210, brands from 6 to 14 - and treat them as the evidence, not as decoration.
Reasoning: each gain needs its because link - prices fall because import competition returns, choice widens because varieties kept out by the tariff enter.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean that for consumers: the same blanket costs less, and there are more blankets to choose between.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: At the border post at Walvis Bay, officials add a charge of N$50 to each imported blanket that crosses. Define a tariff.
items.canonical_answer: A tariff is a tax a government places on imported goods. It raises the price of the import in the home market - the N$50 charge lifts an N$200 blanket to N$250 - and the government collects the charge as revenue. It is one of the four methods of protection, beside import quotas, subsidies and embargoes, and it differs from a quota in that it works through the price rather than through the quantity.
marking_guidance: Definition: the precise meaning required is a tax on imported goods; the example may earn the second mark alongside it.
The boundary worth a word: a tariff taxes each import and raises revenue, whereas a quota caps the quantity directly - naming the difference shows the term is understood rather than pattern-matched.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A government can shelter home blanket makers with a tariff or with an import quota. Explain why a quota may protect them more strongly than a tariff.
items.canonical_answer: A quota protects more strongly because it caps the quantity directly, whatever buyers are willing to pay. A tariff works through price: it lifts the import price, but if buyers keep buying - because they prefer the imported make or the home supply is short - imports keep entering and the shelter leaks. A quota closes that leak: because the quantity itself is fixed at a low level, home producers are certain of the sales the quota reserves for them, however strongly buyers want the import. The purpose of both is the same, but the quota removes the buyer choice that a tariff leaves open.
marking_guidance: Reasons: the reason required is the mechanism - a quota fixes the quantity whatever the price, a tariff only raises it - developed with a because link.
Why: the development should show what happens where buyers keep paying - the tariff shelter weakens while the quota holds - since that is what stronger protection means.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Namibia places an N$80 tariff on each imported shirt, which costs N$320 at the border before the tariff. In the following year imports fall from 20 000 shirts to 15 000, and home shirt makers raise output from 9 000 shirts to 12 000. Explain how the tariff has protected home shirt makers, using the figures.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show the tariff working through the price. The imported shirt rises from N$320 to N$400 at the border, since N$320 + N$80 = N$400, so home shirts become cheaper relative to the import. Buyers respond: imports fall from 20 000 shirts to 15 000, and home makers raise output from 9 000 to 12 000 shirts - 3 000 more, since 12 000 - 9 000 = 3 000. The tariff has protected home shirt makers because the dearer import turns buyers towards home shirts, and their output and sales rise in the year the figures cover.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - the N$80 tariff on the N$320 shirt, imports 20 000 to 15 000, home output 9 000 to 12 000 - as the working material.
Reasoning: the protection needs its because link - the tariff raises the import price, so buyers shift towards home shirts, so home output rises.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean that for home shirt makers: 3 000 more shirts made and sold, because the import stands N$80 dearer.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Namibia solar panel industry started only recently and cannot yet match the prices of panels from established producers abroad. Define an infant industry.
items.canonical_answer: An infant industry is a new domestic industry, not yet large enough to produce at the cost per unit of its established foreign rivals, so it cannot yet compete on price without help. Protection such as a tariff on the imported rival good may shelter it while it grows towards the scale at which its costs fall. The argument for shelter is temporary by design: the protection is there because the industry is young, and may be withdrawn when it matures.
marking_guidance: Meaning: the definition must state a new domestic industry, too small to match established rivals on cost per unit, and may add the temporary shelter of protection while it grows.
The reason it names: infant industry is one of the reasons governments give for protection, so the definition should carry why it is newness that matters - scale has not yet brought costs down.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Imported solar panels cost N$340 each before Namibia places an N$80 tariff on them to shelter its three-year-old panel industry. Analyse how the tariff may help the infant industry reach the scale it needs, and who bears the cost while it grows.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the tariff raises the price of an imported panel from N$340 to N$420, since N$340 + N$80 = N$420. Mechanism: because the import now costs N$80 more, home panels priced near N$400 become competitive, so buyers who mind price tend to switch, and home firms keep the sales they may otherwise have lost to the import. Consequence for the industry: with sales held, output grows, and as output grows the cost per unit tends to fall with scale - each batch of panels spreads its costs over more units - which is the scale the infant industry needs if it is one day to face the import without shelter. For whom: home panel firms and their workers gain sales and jobs while the industry grows; consumers bear the cost, because they pay N$80 more for an imported panel, or a home panel priced close to it, until the industry matures and the shelter is withdrawn.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the analysis must open with the initial change - the tariff lifting the imported panel from N$340 to N$420 - before any consequence is drawn.
Mechanism: the middle marks are for the causal chain - the dearer import turns buyers towards home panels, so home sales and output grow, so cost per unit falls with scale.
Consequence: the chain must land somewhere: the industry moves towards competing without shelter, and the marks follow the therefore, not the listing.
For whom: the answer must name who gains - home firms and workers - and who bears the cost - consumers paying more per panel while the industry grows.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Cement arrives at Walvis Bay priced below the cost of producing it, and home cement makers see their sales fall from 60 000 tonnes a year to 40 000 within a year. Explain why these figures may lead the government to protect the cement industry.
items.canonical_answer: The figures suggest dumping: cement entering priced below its cost of production points to a seller taking the Namibian market by selling at a loss rivals cannot match. The home makers have lost a third of their sales in a year, from 60 000 tonnes to 40 000, and the reason that matters is what follows next: because the loss keeps going, home makers may close, and the country would then depend on the very sellers whose pricing drove them out. The government may therefore protect the industry with a tariff or a quota, because raising the dumped price or capping the quantity keeps the home market for home producers, and the jobs and supply security that go with it.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - sales falling from 60 000 tonnes to 40 000 a year, and the below-cost price - as the evidence of dumping.
Reasoning: protection follows from the reason, not the figures alone: below-cost selling is dumping, so the government acts because uncounted losses lead home producers to close.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean that: a dumped import is taking the market, and protection is the reply that keeps the home industry standing.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: After one country placed a tariff on Namibian beef, Namibia replied with a tariff on that country machinery. Define a retaliatory tariff.
items.canonical_answer: A retaliatory tariff is a tariff one country places on another country goods in answer to a barrier that country has already placed on its exports. It is a consequence of protection rather than a reason for it: the first tariff costs the partner sales, and the partner may answer in kind, so each round tends to shrink trade between the two countries.
marking_guidance: Definition: the precise meaning required is a tariff imposed in response to another country trade barrier - both halves, the tariff and the reply, are needed.
The direction to keep: the retaliation is a consequence of the first barrier, and the answer should carry that direction rather than presenting the reply as a fresh grievance.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: The N$80 tariff on imported shirts has now run for two years. Imports stand at 15 000 shirts a year against 20 000 before the tariff, and home output at 12 000 against 9 000. Analyse the consequences of the tariff for consumers, home shirt makers and the government.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the tariff keeps the imported shirt N$80 above the N$320 it cost before, and the market has settled: imports at 15 000 shirts, home output at 12 000. Mechanism: because the import is dearer, buyers who remain pay more - N$80 more an imported shirt - while home shirts, no longer undercut so easily, tend to sit at a higher price than before. Consequences for each: for consumers, the same shirt costs more and the choice among shirts is narrower, since imports that cannot price in are fewer; for home shirt makers, output stands 3 000 shirts higher than before, since 12 000 - 9 000 = 3 000, and the jobs behind it stay, but the shelter also means less pressure to cut their own costs; for the government, the tariff yields revenue of 15 000 x N$80 = N$1 200 000 a year, which is a transfer from buyers to the state rather than new wealth.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the analysis must open with the standing situation - the N$80 tariff, imports at 15 000, home output at 12 000 - before the consequences are drawn.
Mechanism: the chain must show because the import is dearer, prices and quantities settle where they do, and therefore each party lands where the figures show.
Consequence: each consequence must arrive as a result - consumers pay more, home makers hold 3 000 more shirts of output, the government collects N$1 200 000 a year.
For whom: the three parties must be named - consumers, home shirt makers, the government - and the marks follow the consequence for each rather than a list of prices.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: When the shirt tariff was announced abroad, the exporting country shirt industry cut 900 jobs, and its government began preparing a tariff on Namibian fish. Explain what these facts suggest about the consequences of protection for Namibia trading partners.
items.canonical_answer: The facts suggest the tariff costs the partner directly and invites a cost back. Jobs: the shirt industry abroad cut 900 jobs, because the tariff shrank the market its exports served from 20 000 shirts towards 15 000 - the sales those workers supported moved to Namibia makers or vanished. Retaliation: the partner preparing a tariff on Namibian fish means that the protection is likely to travel back, because its government answers the cost landing on its own industry with a cost of its own for Namibia exporters. Together the facts mean that protection is not a home-only policy: its consequences cross the border, and the reply crosses back.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the facts given - the 900 jobs cut in the exporting country shirt industry, the tariff being prepared on Namibian fish - as its working material.
Reasoning: each consequence needs its because link - jobs go because exports fall, retaliation comes because the partner answers the cost it carries.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the facts mean that for Namibia trading partners: they lose exports and jobs, and they may answer with barriers of their own.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Namibia shirt industry employs 2 000 workers behind the N$80 tariff. Discuss whether the country should keep protecting it.
items.canonical_answer: The case for keeping the protection: 2 000 workers and their households depend on the industry, and because the tariff holds the import N$80 dearer, home output and the jobs behind it stay; behind that shelter an industry that has not yet reached scale may grow towards one that competes without help, which is the infant-industry purpose protection claims. The case against: consumers pay N$80 more an imported shirt, and home shirts tend to sit dearer too, so the cost spreads across every household that buys shirts; the shelter removes the pressure on home makers to cut costs, so an industry that never matures may lean on the tariff indefinitely; and abroad the tariff costs the partner exports and invites retaliation on Namibia own sales, such as fish or beef, so the country may trade less on both sides. Judgement: on balance the protection is worth keeping where the industry is genuinely moving towards standing alone - the condition it depends on is whether the tariff is temporary, with a stated point at which it is withdrawn, or permanent. Where no such point exists, the consumer cost and the retaliation risk settle the case against.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer must reach a reasoned conclusion - on balance, or it depends - not a list of points.
Why it might: the argument for keeping the protection must be developed - the 2 000 jobs, the time to reach scale.
Why it might not: the argument against must be developed with its own weight - the consumer cost, the missing pressure to improve, the retaliation on Namibia exports.

Decisive: what settles it is the condition - whether the tariff is temporary and the industry genuinely maturing, and the strongest answers state what would have to hold for protection to be worth its cost.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Globalisation is best defined as:
A  the spread of multinational companies across the world
B  the growing integration of the world economies through trade, companies and the movement of finance, information and people
C  the removal of all border taxes everywhere
D  the movement of workers from poorer countries to richer ones

2. A multinational company is a firm that:
A  is owned by the government of its home country
B  sells its shares on a stock exchange
C  exports everything it produces
D  produces goods or sells them in more than one country

3. Free trade means:
A  goods cross borders and buyers pay nothing for them
B  trade between neighbouring countries only
C  international trade without government barriers such as tariffs and quotas
D  trade carried by sea rather than by road or air

4. Which is a benefit of free trade for consumers?
A  lower prices and wider choice as imports compete with home goods
B  more tariff revenue for the government
C  larger markets for home producers
D  higher prices that reward home firms for their quality

5. A tariff is:
A  a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
B  a tax on imported goods
C  a payment to home producers that lowers their costs
D  a ban on trade with a particular country

6. An import quota differs from a tariff because a quota:
A  raises revenue for the government on each unit
B  lowers the price of the imported good at the border
C  removes the barrier once home producers are ready
D  caps the quantity imported directly, whatever the price

7. A government shelters a new industry until it grows big enough to produce at a cost per unit close to established rivals. The reason for protection named here is:
A  declining industry
B  dumping
C  infant industry
D  strategic industry

8. A tariff of N$80 is placed on 15 000 imported shirts a year. The revenue it raises is:
A  N$120 000
B  N$12 000
C  N$2 400 000
D  N$1 200 000
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 D, 3 C, 4 A, 5 B, 6 D, 7 C, 8 D.
1. B states the definition - growing integration through trade, companies and movement. A narrows globalisation to one carrier of it, C mistakes a policy choice some countries make for the whole process, D names one flow among several and misses trade, companies and finance.
2. D is the definition - produces or sells in more than one country. A confuses a multinational with a state-owned company, B with a public limited company - the confusion between where it operates and who owns it - and C mistakes exporting for producing or selling abroad, which a purely domestic exporter never does.
3. C states it - trade without government barriers. A is the free trade vs goods being free confusion: free refers to the barriers, not to the price. B mistakes the reach of trade for its freedom, and D mistakes the mode of transport for the policy.
4. A names the consumer benefit - lower prices and wider choice. B answers at the level of the government and C at the level of producers, which is the individuals vs country confusion: the question names consumers, and D reverses the direction of the benefit.
5. B is the definition - a tax on imports. A is the quota, C the subsidy, D the embargo: three of the four methods of protection, swapped for the one asked for.
6. D gives the difference - a quota caps quantity directly. A is the tariff strength, not the quota; B reverses what a border barrier does; C invents a self-removing barrier, and the persistent answer is that a quota holds whatever the price.
7. C - new industry growing towards scale is the infant industry. A is an industry losing ground, B is an exporter pricing below cost, D is security of supply: each is a different reason, and the scale argument names the infant.
8. D - 15 000 x N$80 = N$1 200 000. A drops a zero in the multiplication, B drops two, and C doubles it: each is an arithmetic slip rather than a different method.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question; the correct option for each question is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Distractors that merely restate the question catch nothing; each wrong option traces to a named error - an ownership form read as multinationality, free trade read as goods without price, a consumer benefit answered at the producer or government level, or one protection method swapped for another.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt:
A report from Otavi, 2026. Namibia blanket makers asked two years ago for shelter against imported blankets, and the government replied with a tariff of N$50 on each imported blanket. The figures below show the blanket market in the year before the tariff and last year. Home blanket makers have since raised output from 3 000 to 3 800 blankets.

Table 1 - blankets a year
  imported, year before the tariff: 8 000 blankets at N$200 each
  imported, last year: 6 000 blankets at N$250 each
  home-made, year before the tariff: 3 000 blankets at N$210 each
  home-made, last year: 3 800 blankets at N$230 each
  tariff: N$50 on each imported blanket

(a) Calculate the price of an imported blanket once the tariff is added to the N$200 border price. [1]
(b) Calculate the tariff revenue the government collected last year. [1]
(c) Identify two methods of protection, other than a tariff, the government could have used. [2]
(d) Explain why the tariff may help home blanket makers. [4]
(e) Analyse what the figures suggest the tariff has done to consumers, home producers and the government in Namibia, and how the exporting country blanket makers may respond. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) N$200 + N$50 = N$250. The imported blanket costs the buyer N$250 once the tariff is added.
(b) 6 000 x N$50 = N$300 000. The government collected N$300 000 of tariff revenue last year.
(c) An import quota - a limit on the quantity of blankets that may be imported - and a subsidy - a payment to home blanket makers that lowers their costs. An embargo on blanket imports would also earn credit as a third method.
(d) The tariff adds N$50 to each imported blanket, so the import rises from N$200 to N$250 while home blankets sell at N$230. Because the home blanket is now N$20 cheaper than the import, buyers who mind price tend to switch, so home makers keep and grow their sales - output has risen from 3 000 to 3 800 blankets - and the jobs and income behind those sales stay in Otavi. The tariff helps home blanket makers because it lifts the price of the rival they compete against, which means that their own price wins buyers it was losing before.
(e) Expected relationship: a tariff raises the import price and shifts buying towards home producers, while collecting revenue for the government. Evidence from the data: imports fell from 8 000 blankets to 6 000 while the import price rose from N$200 to N$250; home output rose from 3 000 to 3 800 while the home price rose from N$210 to N$230; the government collected N$300 000. Analysis: consumers pay the rise twice over - N$50 more for an imported blanket, and N$20 more for a home one, because import competition no longer holds the home price down - so the cost lands on buyers across the market, while the benefit concentrates on home producers and the state. Home producers gain 800 blankets of output, since 3 800 - 3 000 = 800, and with it the jobs behind them. The exporting country blanket makers have lost 2 000 blankets of sales, since 8 000 - 6 000 = 2 000, and their likely response is to press their own government for barriers on Namibian exports, which would shrink trade on both sides. Exception: the figures suggest rather than prove - the home output gain may owe something to a colder season or new home capacity, and the price rises to something beyond the tariff - so the tariff share of each change is an inference, not an observation.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) and (b) are 1 mark each and must be exact calculations from Table 1; (c) is 2 marks, one per method named; (d) is 4 marks; (e) is 6 marks.
In (e) award one point per distinct linked statement: expected relationship, evidence from the data, analysis, and an exception all carry marks.
In (e) quoting a figure from Table 1 is evidence, not analysis - a figure without the linked statement it supports earns nothing in (e).
For whom: consequences in (e) are named for consumers, home producers, the government and the exporting country makers.

facts: import price N$200 before, N$250 last year
home price N$210 before, N$230 last year

items.prompt:
Namibia trades freely in most goods but protects its three-year-old solar panel industry.
(a) Define free trade. [2]
(b) Explain two reasons why a government protects an industry from import competition. [4]
(c) Analyse how a tariff on imported solar panels may affect consumers, home panel makers and the government. [6]
(d) Discuss whether protecting an industry from imports benefits a country more than trading freely. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Free trade is international trade without government barriers - no tariffs, no import quotas, no embargoes. The word free refers to the barriers, not to prices: goods traded freely still carry prices and their buyers still pay them. Two creditable elements: trade without barriers, and the boundary of the word free.
(b) Reason one, infant industry: a new industry starts small, so its cost per unit tends to sit above established foreign rivals; protection lifts the import price, so home firms keep sales while they grow towards the scale at which their costs fall. Reason two, anti-dumping: where an exporter sells below its cost of production to take the market, home producers lose sales and may close; a tariff or quota raises the dumped price, so home producers keep their market and their workers keep their jobs. Two reasons, each developed with its because link, earn the four marks.
(c) Starting point: the tariff raises the price of imported panels at the border. Mechanism: because the import is dearer, buyers tend to switch towards home panels, so home makers keep sales they were losing and may raise output, while the jobs behind the output stay. Consequence for each party: consumers pay more for a panel, imported or home, because import competition no longer holds the home price down; home panel makers gain output, sales and room to grow, though the shelter also eases the pressure on them to cut costs; the government collects the tariff as revenue, a transfer from buyers to the state. For whom the analysis must name all three: consumers carry the cost, home makers and their workers hold the benefit, the government holds the revenue.
(d) Why it might benefit more: protection keeps home output and jobs that freer trade may move abroad, which matters where the industry employs whole towns; it gives an infant industry time to reach scale, after which the country may produce competitively without shelter; and it keeps supply secure where the good is strategic, such as food or fuel. Why it might not: consumers across the economy pay higher prices so that one industry can keep its sales, and the cost lands on every household that buys the good; the shelter removes the pressure on home firms to cut costs and improve, so an industry that never matures leans on the tariff indefinitely; and trading partners lose exports and may retaliate with barriers of their own, so the country ends up trading less on both sides. Judgement: on balance protection benefits a country more than free trade where the shelter is genuinely temporary and the industry is moving towards standing alone - the condition it depends on - while where the protection settles into permanence, the consumer cost, the lost pressure to improve and the retaliation risk leave free trade the better servant of the country as a whole.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) 2 marks for two creditable elements of the definition; (b) 4 marks, two per reason developed with its because link; (c) 6 marks, one per distinct linked statement with its reason carried; (d) 8 marks, level-marked over three bands.

Bands for (d): Level 3 (top) examines why it might and why it might not, then reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side of the case; Level 1 asserts points without development.
In (c) the parties must be named - consumers, home panel makers, the government - and each consequence must arrive as a result rather than a list.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "A country that protects its industries from imports serves its people better than one that trades freely." Discuss. Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for protection:
Point 1 - jobs kept. Chain: a tariff lifts the import price -> buyers shift towards home goods -> home output and the jobs behind it stay -> the towns those industries employ keep their income (for workers and their households).
Point 2 - time to reach scale. Chain: an infant industry starts small, so its cost per unit sits above rivals -> shelter holds the import price up -> home firms keep sales while they grow -> costs per unit tend to fall with scale -> the industry may one day stand without shelter (for the industry and the economy).
Case against protection:
Point 1 - consumers pay. Chain: the import price rises -> home prices follow as import competition eases -> households pay more for the same goods -> the cost spreads across every buyer of the good (for consumers, and low-income households hardest).
Point 2 - the reply from abroad. Chain: partner exporters lose sales -> their government may retaliate with barriers of its own -> the country exporters lose the markets they had -> trade shrinks on both sides (for exporters and the economy).
Judgement: protection serves the people better where the shelter is genuinely temporary - where the industry is moving to stand alone and the tariff has a stated end - and the condition it depends on is whether that withdrawal is realistic. Where the protection settles into permanence, the permanent consumer cost and the retaliation risk mean the people are served better by trading freely, with protection kept for the narrow cases of dumping and strategic supply.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the case for, the case against and the stated judgement is what is assessed.
Each point must be developed as a chain from the barrier to its consequence, naming the party it lands on - workers, consumers, exporters, the economy.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: whether the protection is temporary and the industry genuinely maturing.
What settles it: what the shelter buys and whether it is withdrawn once it has bought it - the decisive test is the realistic exit, not the shelter itself.

free trade lowers consumer prices through import competition
